WORD FROM THE AUDITOR-GENERAL
Introduction

I t is my pleasure and honour to present the Annual Corporate Report for the Office of the Auditor-General. This is in pursuant to Article 254 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that after the end of each financial year, a holder of an Independent Office submits a report to the President and to Parliament.

This report gives an account of our performance for the Financial Year 2023/2024 and is based on Article 229 of the Constitution, which outlines the mandate of the Office of the Auditor-General (OAG). As we audit and report on the use and management of public resources, we go beyond the audit of entities, to building public trust in the Office by upholding professionalism and reliability in our work.
Audit Reports Submitted

During the year, we submitted 1,919 financial audit reports to Parliament, comprising 1,047 reports for the National Government and 872 County Governments' reports. We issued sixteen (16) Specialised Audit reports-Six (6) Performance Audits reports, five (5) Forensic Audits reports, four (4) Public Debt Audits reports and (1) Citizen Accountability Audit report.

It is encouraging that Parliament is now considering Performance Audit Reports in addition to the Financial Audit Reports that they have previously been familiar with for a long time. I am glad that our plea to the Members of Parliament to consider the reports the same way they do financial audit reports, is now being addressed. The significant interest and public discourse in our performance audit reports is highly commendable.

I applaud the Speaker of the National Assembly for specifically directing that performance audit reports be prioritised for discussion by Departmental Committees. This has given us impetus to conduct more performance audits in line with our Vision of Making a difference in the lives and livelihoods of Kenyan people.
Achievements
I am pleased to report that during the year, we posted the following key achievements:
Parliament discussed the Performance Audit Report on Provision of Services to Persons with Disability; the first ever Performance audit report to be discussed by a Committee of Parliament;
ii) We transitioned to a more robust webbased Audit Management System (AMS) that has improved efficiency, transparency and accountability in the audit process;
iii)  We developed a Performance Management System to inculcate a high performance culture  and spur productivity in the Office;
Audit Scope

Our audit universe has been increasing and now comprises 12,784 clients.  We have new public sector entities such as hospitals and schools that are now self accounting and required to prepare financial statements for audit.

This expansion of clientele, together with requests from Parliament and our Stakeholders for special audits, requires more resources for timely execution of our audit services. We appeal for increased funding from The National Treasury and Parliament as we seek further support from Development Partners to enable us effectively deliver on our Constitutional mandate.
iv)  We developed a system for tracking and follow-up implementation of recommendations emanating from Parliamentary Committees and the Office;
We also enhanced decentralisation of our audit services by establishing two additional Regional Offices, making them fifteen (15) in total;
vi)  Our Office witnessed an increase in stakeholder interest in our audit services through extensive  media coverage and social media mentions;
vii) We conducted a Stakeholder Satisfaction Survey on Service Delivery which indicated an overall satisfaction level of 75%.
Citizens' Voice

The Office has a fiduciary responsibility to ensure prudent management and use of public resources. Citizens are strategic stakeholders in this noble duty and their involvement in oversight is therefore critical in enhancing accountability and value for money.

As a result, under Citizen Accountability Audits (CAA), we conduct participatory audits where citizens, through communitybased organisations are involved in the audit process to confirm performance and beneficial impact in the management and use of public resources. This ensures that we submit audit reports that are more impactful and address the needs of the people and the requirements of Stakeholders.
Recurring Audit Issues

Every year, we issue audit reports. Unfortunately, often times, the same issues keep recurring. We have concluded through our in-depth analysis that these issues are recurring because recommendations are not being implemented and there are no consequences for failure to implement recommendations.

Accounting Officers must take notice of the issues the AuditorGeneral has been raising and the action taken on those issues, to ensure that they do not recur. When recommendations are not implemented, we cannot be as impactful as we should be as needed change does not occur.
My Office will continue to conduct audits that impact on the lives and livelihoods of the Citizens, by ensuring that our audits are timely, relevant and address issues affecting the citizens.

What we do
The Office of the Auditor-General (OAG) is an Independent Office established by Article 229 of the Constitution of Kenya.

The Office is charged with the primary oversight role of ensuring accountability in the use and management of public resources within the three arms of government (the Legislature, the Judiciary and the Executive) as well as the Constitutional Commissions and Independent Offices. Our oversight role extends to both at the National and County Governments.

Our Audits
During the year, we conducted the following audits:
Financial Audits

These audits examine and evaluate financial statements of public entities to confirm whether they present a true, fair view and transparent disclosure of their transactions. A certificate/an opinion is given.
We carried out 1,919 financial audits comprising 1,047 at the National level and 872 at the County level. These are the clients who submitted their financial statements for auditing:

The Office of the Auditor-General continues to improve  the effectiveness and quality of the audit process to ensure that audit reports and recommendations are credible, relevant, reliable and value adding. This is geared towards influencing improved decision-making and enhancing positive impact on the lives and livelihoods of citizens.
Audit Opinions

In our audit reports, the Auditor-General expresses satisfaction or non-satisfaction of the financial statements through an audit opinion. Opinions expressed depending on the level of transparency, accountability and disclosure  may be as follows:
1. Unqualified Opinion (Unmodified Opinion)

This means that the books of accounts and the supporting records agree with the financial statements presented and no material misstatements have been found. The financial statements present fairly, in all material respects the operations of the audited entity.
2. Qualified Opinion (Modified Opinion)

This means that the recorded financial transactions are to a large extent in agreement with the underlying records, except for cases where material misstatements or omissions in the financial statements are noted. The issues, though deemed material, are not widespread or persistent.
3. Adverse Opinion

This opinion is issued where financial statements exhibit significant misstatements from the underlying accounting records. The financial statements significantly disagree with the underlying books of accounts and/or standards. The problems are widespread, persistent and require considerable interventions by management for rectification.
4. Disclaimer of opinion

This is an opinion issued when financial statements exhibit serious and significant misstatements that may arise from inadequate information, limitation of scope, inadequacy or lack of proper records such that the Auditor-General is not able to form an opinion on the financial operations.

Citizen Accountability Audit

Citizen Accountability Audit entails conducting participatory audits where citizens, through Community-Based Organisations (CBOs), are involved in the audit process to enhance service delivery and good governance principles.

During the year, we conducted an assessment on the level of compliance by counties to relevant legal requirements while providing health care services under the Global Fund Programme and specifically, the extent to which counties;
~ Enabled citizens to access health information;
~ Provided health care services to citizens
~ Ensured that human rights were upheld in the health facilities.

The audit examined implementation of the Global Fund Programme under the Ministry of Health in seven (7) counties (Nairobi, Busia, Bungoma, Homabay, Nyeri, Isiolo and Taita Taveta) and sampled eighteen (18) facilities in these counties. The assessment covered two financial years (2020/2021 and 2021/2022).

The Office continues to engage stakeholders in Citizen Accountability Audits in order to enhance public participation and strengthen trust in our work. The stakeholders who have been brought on board for these types of audits include International Organisations like the World Bank, GIZ, Transparency International, NonGovernmental Organisations (NGOs), Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), CommunityBased Organisations (CBOs) and Faith-Based Organisations (FBOs).

SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being
We carried out a performance audit on Provision of Emergency Medical Care Services in Kajiado County.

The objective of the audit was to assess whether the County Government of Kajiado has ensured timely response and adequate delivery of emergency medical care services. This aligns with SDG 3 Target 3.6 which seeks to halve the number of global deaths and injuries from road traffic accidents by 2030. Further, the audit responds to SDG 3 Target 3.8 which seeks to achieve universal health coverage, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential health-care services and access to safe,
effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all.

The audit established that the County Government of Kajiado has put in place systems towards provision of emergency medical care services. However, the systems in place have not ensured timely response and adequate delivery of emergency medical care services.

The audit recommends that the County Government of Kajiado should ensure that the systems in place are efficient and effective in order to ensure timely response and adequate delivery of emergency medical care services.
SDG 4 : Quality Education

We conducted a performance audit on the National School Meals and Nutrition Programme. The audit addresses SDG 4 Target 4.1 that seeks to ensure that all girls and boys complete free, equitable and quality primary and secondary education leading to relevant and effective learning outcomes by 2030.

The objective of the audit was to assess whether the programme as implemented by the State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education (SDEL&BE) has ensured access to adequate, and quality school meals to pupils in primary schools in arid and semiarid lands, and urban informal settlements in Kenya.

The audit established that the State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education did not ensure access to adequate, safe and nutritious food commodities to feed pupils every school day. The audit recommends for the State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education to carry out continuous market research to ascertain actual cost of a meal, and ensure enrolment data used reflects the actual enrolment in beneficiary schools, so as to inform better planning and budgeting for the programme. Additionally, the State Department for Early Learning and Basic Education should coordinate with relevant stakeholders to explore mechanisms for provision of safe, quality and nutritious school meals.

SDG 6 : Clean Water and Sanitation

We carried out a performance audit on Conservation of Water Towers in Kenya which is in line with SDG 6 Target 6.1 which seeks to achieve universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all, by 2030. The audit is in line with SDG 6 Target 6.6 which sought to protect and restore water-related ecosystems, including mountains, forests, wetlands, rivers, aquifers and lakes, by 2020.
The audit objective was to assess the measures implemented by the government, through the Kenya Water Towers Agency (KWTA), to conserve water towers for sustainable water supply.

The audit revealed that the Agency was yet to undertake a comprehensive survey, mapping and fencing of the gazetted water towers exposing them to encroachment. The Agency had also not identified critical water catchment areas in all the gazetted water towers for protection purposes. Even though the Agency rehabilitated the degraded water towers through tree planting, it was observed that much of the efforts were directed towards non-gazetted water towers.

Focus was not on tree growing and hence the reforested sites registered low seedling survival rates. Due to the inadequacies in protection and rehabilitation activities, the audit revealed that the water towers experienced a decline in forest cover and flow volumes for rivers emanating from the affected water towers.

The audit recommends that the Agency should work closely with the State Department for Environment and Climate Change to fast-track the finalisation and enactment of the Kenya Water Towers Agency Conservation and Coordination Policy, 2019 and Kenya Water Towers Bill, 2019. This would strengthen the Agency's mandate as a lead coordinator and overseer in water conservation. The audit also recommended that the Agency undertakes a comprehensive assessment of the extent of encroachment in all the water towers to facilitate reclamation of the water tower land. The Agency should also develop and implement a guideline on tree planting with emphasis on tree growing .

CHAPTER 3: CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
People and Culture
The Office has made deliberate efforts to attract, retain and develop our staff to enable us achieve our strategic priorities.
The Office recruited 229 staff to support the expanded mandate. OAG has created a positive working environment by providing necessary tools, resources and a conducive learning environment for staff.

Professional Development

Professional development of our staff is a catalyst for effective execution of our mandate. During the year, the Office conducted a number of capacity-building interventions geared towards providing relevant knowledge and skills to enable our staff to deliver on our strategic priorities.

Staff Welfare
People are the greatest  assets for any organisation. Employee welfare is an all-encompassing term that describes the physical and mental health and wellbeing of  employees.

The Office  is cognisant of the importance of  employee welfare. Consequently, we have put in place various welfare initiatives aimed at improving staff motivation, encouraging and promoting healthier attitudes and lifestyles for positive wellbeing of the employees. These include:
Â Provision of adequate office space;
Â Enhanced counselling services to help staff appreciate  work-life balance and manage stress;
Â Enhanced medical scheme;
Â Staff recognition programmes for exemplary performance;
Â Continuous Professional Development (CPD) programmes;
Â Regular feedback mechanisms that allow staff to voice their concerns; and
Â Financial benefits such as enhanced pension plans  to offer financial security to staff postretirement.
Resource Requirement

The Office registered an increase in the number of requests from various stakeholders for special audits on various topics. This, together with the expanded scope of audit, has put a strain on our limited resources.

The Office was allocated Kshs.8.1B to undertake our activities as per the constitutional requirements and our Strategic Plan. This amount was, however, less in comparison to our estimated requirement of Kshs.11.3B leading to a shortfall of about Kshs.3.2B.

Parliament, aware of our need for more resources , recommended that the funding for the Office be based on a formula of onehalf percent (0.5%) of the latest audited and approved revenue figures of the National Government. Currently the latest audited statement of revenue approved by Parliament is for FY 2020/2021 which indicates revenue amount of Kshs.1.7TR.
We continue to appeal to Parliament and The National Treasury for adequate funding to enable us effectively execute our constitutional mandate.
Goods and Services to OAG

We procured goods and services worth KShs.1.05B in line with our Procurement Plan and the Public Procurement and Assets Disposal Act, 2015. Approximately Kshs.63M  worth of contracts were awarded to Youth, Women and Persons with Disabilities.
Facilitating Audit Services

The Office has made strides in improving its Fleet of vehicles to facilitate field visits and verification of projects during audits. During the year, we had a vehicle establishment of 133 against a requirement of 200.
Risk Environment

We reviewed our Risk Management Policy to provide guidance on the management of risks to support the achievement of our strategic objectives. Further, we undertook systems and financial audits across the Office and  followed up on implementation of audit recommendations within various functions in the Office.

In addition, the Office partnered with the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) to undertake a review of its policies, systems and operations with a view to identifying areas that might be prone to corruption and develop strategies of mitigating them.

The Corruption Risk Assessment (CRA) exercise was important in enhancing integrity as it enables organisations to identify and develop appropriate corrective measures to prevent and deal with instances of corruption, proactively.
Compliance with Laws and Regulations
The Office submitted proposals for review of the Public Audit Act, 2015. Some of the proposals have been incorporated in the Public Audit (Amendment) Bill, 2024, currently before Parliament.
The review of the Act was occasioned by the nullification of some sections by the Courts, due to their unconstitutionality as they threatened the independence of the Office.
The review also takes into consideration the evolving public sector environment and enhanced audit standards and methodologies.
Observing quality of our work

In order to improve the quality of our processes, we customised the Quality Assurance Handbook in line with International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI 140). Additionally, the Office developed the Audit Quality Grading System, finalised the Quality Assurance working papers and reviewed guides for financial and performance audit reviews. We also developed Quality Assurance review guides for Institutional Reviews.

Our Engagement Quality Reviewers interact with our work at every stage to ensure quality control in our processes. In line with the strategic priority 1 on enhancing the quality of audit services for improved management of public resources , our Quality Assurance colleagues conduct institutional reviews and individual audit file reviews.

The reviews are meant  to assure the Auditor-General that the system of quality management in place is working well and where there are deficiencies, provide recommendations for improved audits and other functions of the Office. Thus, Quality Assurance reviews assist the Office achieve its mandate, respond to the needs of stakeholders, and enhance accountability and better utilisation of public resources for improved  lives and livelihoods of citizens.

blocks.text: Engaging the Citizens

The Office interacted with Citizens through various channels, including media, public forums, and Citizen Accountability Audits (CAA). During these forums, we addressed inquiries related to our mandate, the audit process, audit opinions and follow-up on audit recommendations.

As part of our commitment to transparency, we continue to translate National Government Audit reports into Kiswahili language and simplify them to enhance our stakeholder reach. Ultimately, the engagement and access of the audit reports enhances citizen participation in decision-making.
Citizens access our audit reports mainly from the website, which is the primary source of information.
Media engagements
We trained 125 journalists across the country to enhance their understanding of

our mandate with special focus on the audit process and audit terminologies to enable them to report accurately. The training was a culmination  of five feedback sessions (media receptions) we held with journalists. These engagements sought feedback and insights on our relationship with the media.
Journalists' Perception of our work
We interviewed 36 journalists from various media houses on their perception of our work.

As we strive to provide impactful audit services, 44% of the journalists rated our work as above average in influencing beneficial change in the society. 56% of the journalists rated the quality of our reports as excellent in enhancing their reporting on public accountability.
In addition, 56% of the respondents rated the accessibility of our reports as excellent while 39% of them rated the understandability of the audit reports as excellent.
We shall endeavour to increase the number of engagements with journalists to have indepth understanding of their needs and develop strategies to address them.
Accuracy of Media Reports

The Office continually assesses the accuracy of reporting by journalists trained in covering audit findings. This allows us to develop suitable interventions to promote objective reporting and improve future media interactions. We have noticed a positive trend, with many journalists interpreting audit reports accurately and effectively sharing relevant information with stakeholders. Sessions with Auditees

We held four feedback sessions with Principal Secretaries, CEOs of State Corporations, Accounting Officers for Technical and Vocational Education and Training Institutions, and Accounting Officers for Municipal and City Boards.  During these engagements, we provided explanations on the audit process and critical areas to focus during audit. We also received feedback on their experience with auditors.
Working with Development Partners
Our Development Partners supported our activities through budgetary support, coordination of programmes and assistance on technical and capacity-building.

During the year, we partnered with; the African Development Bank (AfDB), German Development Agency - Deutsche Geselleschaft fur international Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), World Bank, Agence Francaise de Development (AFD), The Global Fund, the Swedish National Office (SNAO), United Kingdom National Audit Office (UK-NAO), the Public Finance Management Reforms Programme (PFMR)- Kenya and the Horn of Africa Gateway Development Project (HoAGDP).
Feedback from our Stakeholders

Stakeholder feedback is a valuable guide in our work, and assist us in gauging the impact of our services which ensures we develop requisite strategies to meet their expectations. We conducted a survey to assess level of stakeholder satisfaction with our services to get feedback on our audit services.

The Objective of the survey was to establish the level of awareness, satisfaction and perception of stakeholders on OAG services and audit reports. We sought feedback on our independence, impact of our audit reports, quality of our reports, brand visibility and how effectively we communicate with our stakeholders.

The survey targeted 1,200 stakeholders and 1,640 staff members. The total number of participants was 797 external stakeholders and 440 staff members, giving a response rate of 66.4% and 26.8% respectively. The margin of error for the survey was ±1.36%. The survey was conducted between the months of June and August 2023.

A pilot study was conducted to ascertain the reliability of the data collection tool. 12 stakeholders and 8 staff members were involved in the pilot study. Cronbach's Alpha was used to assess the internal consistency of the survey, indicating how well the items measure the same construct. The calculated Cronbach's Alpha was 0.88 giving an excellent level of reliability.

blocks.text: We engaged in various Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability activities as part of our responsibility in giving back to Society. The giving back to society mantra has connected the Office with vulnerable groups besides enhancing good corporate citizenship, creating awareness of our mandate and building trust and positive relationships with our stakeholders.

blocks.text: Case studies

In April 2024, the Office proactively responded to environment and climate change challenges by participating in a tree growing exercise where over 1,200 mangrove seedlings were planted as part of our CSR initiatives. Tree growing is one of the best mitigation actions against Climate Change. The Auditor-General FCPA Nancy Gathungu, CBS launched the exercise at the Majaoni Centre in Mombasa.

She was accompanied by the Migori County Women Representative, Honourable Mohammed Fatuma Zainab, Deputy Auditor Generals, and other staff from the Office. Our staff from Mombasa and Kilifi Regional Offices also participated in the excercise. The Office is partnering with the Kenya Forest Service to provide after-planting care and management of the seedlings as they grow to maturity.

The Office staff also engaged in various CSR activities whenever they went out auditing and capacity-building activities. In June 2024, during the recent audit of public secondary schools, a team assigned to Nyeri County, along with the Headmistress, teachers and others staff members planted indigenous trees at Gatugi Primary School in Othaya. During the same month, staff participating in a syllabus for Audit Methodology Training visited a Children's Home in Embu County and donated assorted foodstuffs and other items in support of the vulnerable children.

The Office analyses its audience in line with its CSR Policy and the constitutional requirement on sustainable development while considering available budgetary allocations, to settle on suitable projects to engage in. The initiatives to support the needy and worthy causes in society are usually realised through voluntary donations and financial contributions from the OAG staff and other well-wishers.
Impact of our Work

Our work continued to elicit interest and attention from our Stakeholders. We registered mentions in the media and other public spaces, where topical issues made reference to some of our reports. Some of the highlights are:
~ Our Performance Audit Report on Prevention and Response to Gender Based Violence was used in an online mini campaign by International Organisation
of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI) Development Initiative (IDI) during a 16-day period of activism against gender-based violence.

~ The Auditor-General's Performance Audit Report on Response to Floods in Kenya attracted 3,383 views on our social media platforms and was used by the media to rally for implementation of audit recommendations in order to prevent or mitigate against the flooding menace that led to loss of lives and displacement of people.

~ Our Financial Audit Reports were the most sought-after information on public accountability based on the number of users who viewed the posts on our social media platforms. The Auditor-General's Report on the County Governments Executives 2022-2023 registered the highest number of users at 5,081 views on X followed by an update on the National Assembly Speaker's communication directing Parliamentary Committees to prioritise discussion of the Performance Audit Reports, which attracted 4,790 views on X.

Resource Persons

We value knowledge and experience sharing within the global public sector auditing community. Our pool of resource persons in Financial and Performance Audits, Communication, Human Resource, Monitoring and Evaluation continue to share their experiences in various AFROSAI-E and IDI programmes meant to support and build capacity for various SAIs.
International Cooperation

We derive value in working with partners to transform the lives and livelihoods of the citizens. Cooperation with partners therefore play a significant role in this mission and we are acknowledged to be part of such cooperation agreements.

Our partnership with the Swedish National Audit Office ( Riksrevisionen), under the East African Regional Cooperation, has registered significant milestones in the areas of Parliamentary Liaison, Quality Assurance, Communication, Performance Audit, and Information Systems and Data Science.  The Cooperation brings together the Supreme Audit Institutions of Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania and Rwanda.

In the same spirit, we are working with the National Audit Office of the United Kingdom to build effective relationships with Parliament and measure audit impact for purposes of reporting on our annual performance.
HIGHLIGHTS
Recognition in HR Practices

We were recognised by AFROSAI-E and bestowed the Excellence Award during the 18 th  AFROSAI-E's Technical Conference on 9 November, 2023. The Award recognised us for excellence in adhering to free and fair internationally recognised recruitment practices. The Award was informed by the OAG's exceptional dedication to advancing its recruitment process.
Professional and Leadership Awards

Our Auditor-General was awarded the Fellowship title by the Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Kenya (ICPAK), for exemplary contribution to the Accounting profession. The Award is the highest recognition for individuals who have made outstanding contributions to the accounting profession.

The Auditor-General was also awarded for being one of the outstanding women in leadership within the public sector in the country. She was recognised and celebrated for her exemplary efforts in enhancing accountability in the use and management of public resources.

The Award is a testament of her dedication to serving citizens in line with the Office's Vision of 'Making a difference in the lives and livelihoods of Kenyan people' . The AG received the Award during a special event for 'Celebrating Women in Leadership' in commemoration of the International Women's Day at the University of Nairobi (UoN), organised by the African Women Studies Centre and the Women's Economic Empowerment (WEE) hub, in collaboration with the UoN.

The occasion honoured and celebrated women who have excelled in leadership roles, acknowledging those who have broken barriers in traditionally male dominated spaces, and provided a platform for mentoring the next generation of women leaders.

Similarly, the Auditor-General, was honoured with the Billy Mwencha Award . The Award was bestowed to her by the Institute of Internal Auditors, and it is given to institutions that have contributed to the advancement and growth of the Internal Audit Profession in Kenya.

The Award is named in honour of Billy Mwencha, former Chairman of the Board of Institute of Internal Auditors-Kenya, and a driving force behind the development of the Internal Audit profession in Kenya.
Our Contribution to Climate Change

Our Staff are members of  the International Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI) Executive Group that developed the ClimateScanner Tool. The Group is composed of 18 Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) from different regions in the world.

The ClimateScanner Project is a global initiative by Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) for rapid assessment of governments' actions to address climate change. The Project aims to achieve the following objectives:
Assess national governments' action on climate change;
Consolidate data in a global overview showing the areas of strengths and challenges on climate action;
Communicate relevant information in an easily understandable manner;
Support decision for future audit work by SAIs; and
Contribute to INTOSAI's global voice on climate change

The project is being implemented in more than 100 countries across the world. The goal is to present a consolidated report during the 29 th Conference of Parties (COP29) in Azerbaijan, highlighting the areas of strengths and challenges on climate action.

blocks.text: Our Challenges
In carrying out our role, we face the following operational challenges;
1. Inadequate budgetary allocations and late disbursements
heading_path: 1. Inadequate budgetary allocations and late disbursements

blocks.text: During 2023/2024, the Office was allocated Kshs. 8.1Billion against our requirement of Kshs11.4 Billion, translating to a funding gap of Kshs 3.3Billion. This, together with delays in Exchequer releases affected the implementation of planned activities. We however, continue to seek support from The National Treasury and Parliament for enhanced budgetary allocation.
heading_path: 1. Inadequate budgetary allocations and late disbursements

blocks.text: 2. Increase in our audit universe

Our audit universe has been increasing over the years as citizens continue to grow interest in enhancing accountability in the use and management of public resources. The zeal for accountability has resulted to numerous requests for special audits by our stakeholders on topical areas, thereby increasing our scope of work.
3. Delay by Parliament to discuss Performance Audit Reports
heading_path: 3. Delay by Parliament to discuss Performance Audit Reports

blocks.text: Despite submitting 63 Performance Audit Reports to Parliament since 2012, only one report has been discussed by Parliament. During 2023-2024, we submitted six audit reports to Parliament, none of which have been discussed by Parliament. The reports give recommendations that, if implemented, would address some of the challenges the country experiences. We acknowledge that the Speaker of the National Assembly, aware of the importance of these reports in transforming the lives of Kenyans, communicated to Parliamentary Committees on 13 May 2024 May to prioritise discussion and adoption of performance audit reports for action.
heading_path: 3. Delay by Parliament to discuss Performance Audit Reports

blocks.text: 4. Low Implementation of Audit Recommendations

The Office and Parliament makes recommendations to enhance the accountability and effective utilisation of public resources. Unfortunately, these recommendations are not always implemented due to lack of follow-up and enforcement mechanisms.

In line with our Mission of Audit services that impact on effective and sustainable service delivery, we have taken proactive measures to develop a framework for tracking, follow-up and reporting on implementation of audit recommendations.

The framework proposes a multi-agency approach to effectively implement the recommendations. Additionally, we have submitted recommendations to Parliament to review the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, to make implementation of audit recommendations mandatory for all public entities and introduce and enforce sanctions to those who fail to comply.
5. Tight Audit Timelines

Our timelines for submission of audit reports to Parliament and County Assemblies are very tight owing to a provision of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, which gives public entities three (3) months after the end of the financial year to present their financial statements for auditing. This reduces the duration to 3 months from the 6 months constitutional timelines given to the AuditorGeneral to audit and report.
CHAPTER 5: ASSESSMENT OF OUR OPERATIONS

The Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) of the African Organisation of English-speaking Supreme Audit Institutions (AFROSAI-E) annually conduct self assessment using the Institutional Capacity Building Framework (ICBF), a tool that enables SAIs to consider and prioritise their capacity building needs, gaps and challenges.
The ICBF assesses the level of development of SAIs on five domain areas:
~ Independence and Legal Framework This assesses the operational, financial and administrative independence of the Auditor-General and the staff.
~ Organisation and Management This focuses on the governance and leadership matters as well as operational and strategic planning.

~ Human ResourcesThis domain assesses management and development of staff. It covers recruitment, induction, retention, recognition, performance management, training, career development and staff wellness.

~ Audit Standards and Methodology This focuses on development, implementation and maintenance of appropriate up-to-date ISSAI compliant audit tools like manuals, guidelines, and templates, in accordance with the SAI's mandate and national legislative requirements.

~ Communication and Stakeholder ManagementThis domain focuses on engagement with stakeholders guided by strategies and plans that are aligned with, and in support of the strategic goals and mandate of the SAI.
An assessment questionnaire was administered to assess the levels of development in the five domains. The development levels are graded from Level 1 to 5, with the following explanations:
Level 1

This is the foundation Level. When a SAI scores Level 1, it means the SAI exists but operations are  at rudimentary Level. The SAI is part of the executive government structure and not independent in any area. The audit work is not organised according to a strategic, annual operational or audit work plan and the work is not carried out according to the INTOSAI Code of Ethics.
Level 2

This is the development Level. The SAI exists and has some legal provisions for its independence, but this provision is not adequate and the SAI is dependent on the executive for its human and financial resources. The Head of the SAI is appointed by the Executive. Access to information, discretion to select audit topics, freedom to decide on content, timing and publishing of reports can be provided by the legislation, but is not carried out without obstacles. The SAI has no direct access to parliament to submit audit reports. Strategic, annual operational, audit, development and communication plans and the thinking behind these can be under planning or development but are not implemented.
Level 3

This is the established Level. At this Level plans prepared or under development at Level 2 are implemented at Level 3, however improvement in some areas or in the implementation is needed. The SAI has a legislative, administrative/managerial and financial independence. The SAI reports directly to Parliament. The Head of SAI is appointed by and can only be removed by Parliament. Functional strategic and operational plans are implemented as well as important quality control requirements for the SAI as set by the Top Management.
Level 4

This is the managed Level. At this Level full compliance with all requirements on Level 3 is achieved by the SAI. The SAI and the key stakeholders are fully satisfied at Level 4 with the implementation of plans and procedures. In addition to the conditions at level 3, the SAI is capable of managing its core business in the most cost efficient and cost-effective way.
Level 5

This is the optimised Level.  The SAI complies fully with all requirements on Level 4. At this Level, the SAI is able to scan the environment and position itself and use the resources in the most proactive and value adding way. To optimise its use of resources the SAI must constantly evaluate, analyse and assess its policies, objectives, strategies, systems, procedures, capacity, the skill of its staff and the impact of its decisions.

Legal Management System

We are developing a Legal Management System that shall address workflow automation, documents management, legal calendaring, case management, contract management and lease management. The system shall improve our efficiency in managing our processes as an Office.
CHAPTER 6: FUTURE PLANS
Citizen Accountability Audit Mobile App

The app is meant to compliment other avenues of engaging with citizens for robust and targeted dissemination of results of CAA operations and policies. The portal and the mobile application will improve OAG's visibility and support the institution's outreach to stakeholders and citizens at large. It will also be used as a knowledge and resource sharing platform, cataloguing and disseminating information for the benefit of citizens.

In addition, the Office of the Auditor-General Kenya has been selected by AFROSAI as one the countries in Africa to implement technology-based solutions to engage citizens and obtain feedback. Other Supreme Audit Institutions selected to implement this programme are Botswana, Rwanda and Liberia. This programme is being supported by GIZ South Africa.
